core_intuitions: Three ALGORITHMIC forces (massive over-training, aggressive data curation, architecture+optimizer transfer) — not hardware — explain why a 2026 100M model is categorically better than a 2019 GPT-2 at the same parameter count.

Compute-optimal is not deployment-optimal: Chinchilla minimizes loss per one-time TRAINING FLOP, but inference recurs forever, so at a fixed (cheap) parameter count you deliberately over-train past Chinchilla because the training cost amortizes over many inference calls.

Where ~101M parameters actually go: the tied embedding table vs 30 deep-thin transformer blocks; GQA makes the K/V projections thin (d_kv=128) while Q/O stay full-width; tied embeddings save ~16.8M (a sixth of the model).
Deep-and-thin (MobileLLM): at a FIXED parameter budget, many narrow layers (30 x d=512) beat fewer wide ones (12 x d=1024).

The whole capstone is ONE growing artifact (package stacklm) taken through the full lifecycle: data -> tokenizer -> architecture -> scaling laws -> optimizer -> pretrain -> mid-train -> post-train -> agent -> eval/serve.
'Narrow but real': the honest target is verifiable narrow-domain competence (calculator, retrieval-grounded QA), not a general chatbot.

new_figures.name: three-forces-2019-to-2026
new_figures.concept: The chapter's thesis in one frame: same parameter count, categorically better model, via three algorithmic forces.
new_figures.rationale: This is the central argument of the entire chapter (the '## Three Forces' section plus the opening Karpathy framing). A reader who groks this one image understands why the whole capstone is worth doing. A static side-by-side with three labeled transformation arrows makes the before/after and the three levers legible at a glance in a way the prose spreads across three subsections.
new_figures.placement: Three Forces That Made Small Models Good
new_figures.brief: A left-to-right transformation infographic. LEFT card: 'GPT-2 124M (2019)' listing its properties as small labeled rows: ~10B tokens (~80 tokens/param); lightly-filtered WebText (Reddit-karma links); learned absolute positions, LayerNorm, GELU MLP, full multi-head attention; plain SGD/Adam + cosine. RIGHT card: 'Stack-100M (2026)' with the parallel rows: ~20B tokens (~200 tokens/param); FineWeb-Edu classifier-filtered + Cosmopedia synthetic; RoPE+NoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, GQA + QK-norm; Muon+AdamW hybrid + WSD schedule. Between the two cards, three large stacked arrows spanning left->right, each labeled as a force: (1) 'Massive over-training — ~10x past Chinchilla-optimal', (2) 'Data quality over quantity — curated + synthetic', (3) 'Architecture + optimizer transfer from frontier labs'. A banner strip beneath or above the arrows reads: 'Same parameter count (~100M) -> categorically better model'. A small footnote flag: 'these are algorithmic choices, not hardware — the same recipe on 2019 GPUs still wins.' Keep the two cards visually symmetric so the row-by-row contrast is obvious. Theme-safe: neutral card fills, a single accent color for the three force arrows; small illustrative integers only (80, 200, ~10B, ~20B) — no invented benchmark scores.

new_figures.name: compute-vs-deployment-optimal
new_figures.concept: Why deliberately over-train past Chinchilla: training is a one-time cost, inference recurs on every call, so at fixed serving cost the smaller over-trained model wins over its lifetime.
new_figures.rationale: The chapter names this 'the single most important economic idea in this capstone' and returns to it in the Interview Corner. The intuition — a crossover between one-time training compute and forever-recurring inference compute — is exactly the kind of thing a single static frame conveys far better than prose, because it is fundamentally about two cost curves crossing.
new_figures.brief: Two stacked panels sharing the theme. TOP (small) panel: a loss-vs-tokens curve (loss decreasing, flattening) for a FIXED parameter count. Mark two points on it: 'Chinchilla-optimal (~20 tokens/param, ~2B)' near the knee, and 'Stack-100M (~200 tokens/param, ~20B)' further right and lower. A short arrow between them labeled 'keep training: loss still drops — just less per training FLOP.' Caption: 'Chinchilla minimizes loss per unit of TRAINING compute only.' BOTTOM (main) panel: the economics. X-axis = 'number of inference calls served (deployment lifetime)', Y-axis = 'cumulative compute cost'. Two straight-ish lines: 'Larger compute-optimal model' starts LOW at x=0 (cheap one-time training) but has a STEEP slope (expensive per-call inference, more parameters); 'Smaller over-trained model' starts HIGHER at x=0 (more one-time training FLOPs) but a SHALLOW slope (cheap to serve at fixed small parameter count). The two lines cross; mark the crossover with a dashed vertical line labeled 'amortization point' and shade the region to the right 'over-trained small model wins here — the deployment regime.' Small annotation: 'training = one-time; inference = recurs on every call forever.' Use one accent per line, theme-safe neutrals for axes and shading; only illustrative integers (20, 200, 2B, 20B), no dollar figures baked into the drawing.

new_figures.name: stack100m-param-budget
new_figures.concept: The hand-verifiable parameter budget: tied embedding vs 30 deep-thin blocks, and the GQA-shaped attention (Q/O full-width, K/V thin).
new_figures.rationale: The chapter's ethos is 'never take ~101M on faith' — it derives the count by hand and in code. A proportional breakdown makes the accounting tangible: it shows at a glance that the tied embedding is a sixth of the model, that depth (30 stacked blocks) dominates, and — via the attention zoom — WHY GQA attention is 2d^2+2*d*d_kv rather than 4d^2. This turns an equation into a picture.
new_figures.placement: Verifying the parameter count by hand
new_figures.brief: A three-level proportional breakdown reading left-to-right (or top-down). LEVEL 1: a single tall stacked bar of the whole ~101M model split into 'Tied embedding table 16.8M (~16.6%)', '30 transformer blocks ~84.6M', and a hairline 'final norm ~0.0005M'. A callout on the embedding segment: 'tied input+output — saves ~16.8M (a sixth of the model)'. LEVEL 2: expand the '30 blocks' segment into a short stack of identical thin layer slabs (emphasize DEPTH — 30 narrow slabs, labeled 'deep-and-thin: 30 layers at d=512, not 12 at d=1024'), and pull ONE block out to the side showing its ~2.82M split: 'SwiGLU MLP 2.163M' (largest), 'GQA attention 0.655M', 'norms ~0.001M'. LEVEL 3: expand the GQA attention into four projection rectangles drawn to WIDTH-scale: Q (d x d, full width) and O (d x d, full width) as wide rectangles; K and V (d x d_kv=128) as visibly THIN rectangles — with the label 'GQA: K,V only n_kv*head_dim=128 wide -> attention = 2d^2 + 2*d*d_kv, NOT 4d^2'. Add a small side note comparing vocab choices: '32768 table = ~16.6% of model; a 50000 table = ~25% (a quarter)'. Theme-safe: segments in a graduated neutral+accent scale, the thin K/V rectangles clearly narrower than Q/O; only the spec's own integers (32768, 512, 30, 128, 16.8M, 84.6M, 2.82M) — invent nothing.

Between them, chained stage nodes in chapter order, each showing the chapter number, its focus, and the concrete ARTIFACT it produces (small caption under each): 14.2 Pretraining data -> packed .bin shards; 14.3 Tokenizer -> 32,768 byte-level BPE; 14.4 Architecture -> the deep-thin transformer; 14.5 Mini scaling laws -> a fitted L(N,D) justifying 101M/20B; 14.6 Optimizer & schedule -> Muon+AdamW + WSD; 14.7 Pretraining loop -> the base model (~20B tokens); 14.8 Mid-training -> annealed weights, 8192 context; 14.9 Post-training -> SFT + DPO + RLVR/GRPO; 14.10 Agentic -> ReAct tool-use, distilled trajectories; 14.11 Eval & serving -> int4 quantized, laptop inference. summary: This is a concept-rich, figure-poor overview/map chapter with ZERO existing figures, so no audit was needed. It carries several strong intuitions that are currently carried entirely by prose and tables. I propose 4 disciplined STATIC figures (none genuinely needs motion): (1) the three-forces 2019->2026 thesis diagram — the chapter's central argument; (2) compute-optimal vs deployment-optimal — a two-panel cost-crossover that makes the capstone's 'single most important economic idea' visceral; (3) a hand-verifiable parameter-budget breakdown that also shows WHY GQA attention is 2d^2+2*d*d_kv (thin K/V) and how tied embeddings save a sixth of the model; and (4) the Part XIV lifecycle arc showing one growing artifact flowing raw-text-in to agent-out. Priorities 1/1/1/2. Deliberately not proposing a FLOPs->dollars figure — the prose worked example is self-contained and clear — keeping the set to the foundational few.
